templates.pattern: A file has an original size of [ORIG] KB and a compressed size of [COMP] KB. Calculate the compression ratio.
templates.explanation:
Compression ratio = original size ÷ compressed size
= [ORIG] ÷ [COMP]
= [RESULT]

A compression ratio of 4 means the compressed file is 4 times smaller than the original. Higher ratios mean better compression.

templates.pattern: A file has an original size of [ORIG] KB and is compressed to [COMP] KB. Calculate the space saving as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Space saving % = (1 − compressed ÷ original) × 100
= (1 − [COMP] ÷ [ORIG]) × 100
= [RESULT]%

A 75% space saving means the compressed file is only 25% of the original size. This is useful for comparing different compression algorithms.

templates.pattern: An audio file has a sample rate of [SR] Hz, a bit depth of [BD] bits and a duration of [DUR] seconds. Calculate the file size in kilobytes (KB).
templates.explanation:
File size = sample rate × bit depth × duration ÷ 8 ÷ 1024
= [SR] × [BD] × [DUR] ÷ 8 ÷ 1024
= [RESULT] KB

Audio file size grows linearly with duration, sample rate and bit depth. CD quality audio (44100 Hz, 16-bit) uses about 10 MB per minute.

templates.pattern: A video has a frame rate of [FPS] frames per second, resolution [W]×[H] pixels and colour depth of [D] bits. Calculate the file size of one minute of video in megabytes (MB).
templates.explanation:
Video file size = FPS × W × H × colour depth × duration ÷ 8 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024
= [FPS] × [W] × [H] × [D] × 60 ÷ 8 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024
= [RESULT] MB

Uncompressed HD video generates enormous file sizes — this is why video compression is essential.

templates.pattern: A file of [SIZE] MB needs to be transmitted. The available bandwidth is [BW] MB/s. Calculate the transmission time in seconds.
templates.explanation:
Transmission time = file size ÷ bandwidth
= [SIZE] ÷ [BW]
= [RESULT] s

Transmission time is directly proportional to file size and inversely proportional to bandwidth. Doubling bandwidth halves transmission time.

templates.pattern: A file of [SIZE] MB needs to be transmitted in [TIME] seconds. Calculate the minimum bandwidth required in MB/s.
templates.explanation:
Bandwidth required = file size ÷ time
= [SIZE] ÷ [TIME]
= [RESULT] MB/s

This calculation is used when designing networks — you need to know the minimum bandwidth to meet a transmission time requirement.

templates.pattern: A digital camera produces images with a resolution of [W] × [H] pixels. Calculate the resolution of the camera in megapixels.
templates.explanation:
Megapixels = width × height ÷ 1,000,000
= [W] × [H] ÷ 1,000,000
= [W*H] ÷ 1,000,000
= [RESULT] MP

Megapixels measure the total number of pixels in millions. More megapixels means higher resolution and more detail but also larger file sizes.

templates.pattern: A video file has [FRAMES] total frames and a duration of [DUR] seconds. Calculate the frame rate in frames per second (fps).
templates.explanation:
Frame rate = total frames ÷ duration
= [FRAMES] ÷ [DUR]
= [RESULT] fps

Higher frame rates produce smoother video. Movies use 24 fps, PAL TV uses 25 fps and modern gaming targets 60 fps or higher.

templates.pattern: A colour image uses [BPC] bits per colour channel and has [CH] colour channels. Calculate the colour depth in bits per pixel.
templates.explanation:
Colour depth = bits per channel × number of channels
= [BPC] × [CH]
= [RESULT] bits per pixel

RGB images use 3 channels (red, green, blue). RGBA adds an alpha channel for transparency. Professional cameras use 10 or 12 bits per channel for greater colour precision.

templates.pattern: A file has a total size of [TOTAL] KB of which [META] KB is metadata. Calculate the metadata overhead as a percentage of the total file size.
templates.explanation:
Metadata overhead % = (metadata ÷ total size) × 100
= ([META] ÷ [TOTAL]) × 100
= [RESULT]%

Metadata stores information about the file — creation date, author, dimensions etc. It adds overhead but is essential for file management and compatibility.
